opus-5.5.text:
I think research taste is one of those things that's really hard to teach directly, but you can absolutely accelerate it.

The first thing I'd say is to get your hands dirty as early as possible. A lot of taste comes from having run enough experiments that you develop an intuition for what's going to work and what's a dead end. You start to notice when a result is too good to be true, or when a curve looks off, and that only comes from reps. People who spend all their time reading papers and not enough time actually training models tend to have a distorted sense of what matters.

The second thing is to be around people who have good taste and pay attention to the questions they ask. In a lot of reviews, the most valuable part isn't the answer someone gives you. It's the question they ask that you hadn't thought to ask yourself. Is this going to scale? What's the simplest baseline that might beat this? Are we fooling ourselves with this eval? Over time you internalize those questions, and that's a big part of what taste is.

Third, I'd really emphasize simplicity. A lot of the ideas that have mattered in this field are almost embarrassingly simple in hindsight. They're things like scaling something up, cleaning the data, or finding the right objective. Early researchers often gravitate toward complicated, clever methods because they feel more like research. But good taste often means asking what the simplest thing is that could possibly work, and then pushing it really hard.

And finally, pick problems you care about over long time horizons. Taste is partly about knowing what's important, not just what's tractable. If you only chase what's publishable in the next three months, you'll get good at incremental work. If you ask what really needs to be true for these systems to get much more capable, and work backward from there, you develop a much sharper sense of which problems are worth your time.

So, in short: lots of experiments, learn from people whose judgment you trust, bias toward simple ideas, and keep your eye on the problems that really matter.

r001.rationale: The response recommends hands-on experiments but does not recommend fully replicating admired research papers.

r002.rationale: It does not say that replication can reveal techniques researchers leave unmentioned.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that taste is mostly something you absorb rather than something you're taught. When I came into the field, I didn't have a formal ML background, I'd been a quant trader. What helped me more than anything was being around people who had taste and watching how they made decisions. Not just what problems they picked, but what they got excited about, what they dismissed quickly, and why.

So my first piece of advice is: optimize for who you work with early on. If you can be in a room where people are arguing about what matters, and you're forced to defend your own choices, you'll develop taste much faster than you would reading papers alone.

The second thing is to actually run a lot of experiments. There's a tendency for people to spend months theorizing about what the right research direction is. But in this field, your intuitions get calibrated by seeing what works and what doesn't. A lot of the ideas that sound great on paper fall apart on contact with a GPU, and a lot of things that feel too simple turn out to be the whole story. You only learn that distinction by getting your hands dirty.

Third, I'd say develop a bias toward problems where you'd be happy with either outcome. If the experiment fails and you learn something real, that's a good project. If the only interesting result is the one where you're right, you're probably picking problems that are too narrow or too incremental.

And then, I think the big one is that taste is downstream of having a view about where the field is going. Ask yourself what will matter in two or three years, not what the hot paper is this month. Scaling was like that. Early on, a lot of very smart people thought it was unglamorous. The people who had the conviction to work on it anyway were drawing on a model of the world, not following the crowd. So try to form your own model, write it down, and then check it against reality every few months. That feedback loop is what taste actually is.

r001.rationale: The response recommends working with people, running experiments, and forming a view of the field, but does not recommend fully replicating admired papers.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from experiments generally, but does not say that replicating results can reveal techniques researchers leave unstated.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste develops through doing research and getting feedback on your intuitions. You pick a problem, you have some reason to believe an approach will work, and then you run the experiment. When it doesn’t work, understanding why is often where you learn the most.

For someone starting out, I’d suggest keeping that loop short. Find a question where you can test something in a week or two. Before you run it, write down what you expect to happen and why. That helps you distinguish between actually having a useful intuition and explaining the result after the fact.

It also helps to work with people whose judgment you respect. Ask why they’re excited about one problem and passing on another. A paper usually gives you the polished argument; those conversations expose the uncertainty and the choices behind it.

Over time, you develop a sense of which questions are both important and tractable. But you need some room to follow your own curiosity, too. If you only work on things everyone already agrees are promising, it’s hard to develop an independent point of view.

r001.rationale: The response recommends short experiments and learning from feedback, but it does not advise fully replicating admired papers.

r002.rationale: It says conversations with experienced researchers reveal uncertainty and choices behind their work, but does not state that replication reveals techniques left undisclosed in papers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste is something you develop by actually doing research. You pick a problem, you have some intuition about what might work, and then you run the experiment. And often you’re wrong. But that gap between what you expected and what happened is where you start to build intuition.

When you’re starting out, it helps to work with people whose judgment you respect. Try to understand why they’re excited about a particular question. What do they see that you don’t? And then make your own predictions before you see the results, so you can actually calibrate your judgment.

I’d also give yourself room to follow things that seem interesting even if you can’t fully explain why yet. You need enough persistence to get past the first failed experiment, but enough honesty to recognize when the evidence is telling you to change direction. Learning that balance is a big part of developing taste.

r001.rationale: The response recommends doing research and learning from respected researchers, but it does not recommend fully replicating admired papers.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning from experiment outcomes, but does not say replication can uncover techniques researchers leave unmentioned.
